report.intro_body: This report presents an executive summary of the security activity detected by Heimdall Community, the free honeypot platform by AllSafe Security Solutions, during the selected period. A honeypot is a decoy system: it exposes fake services that no legitimate user has any reason to use, so all the traffic it records is, by definition, unsolicited and potentially hostile. The purpose of this document is to provide clear visibility into who is probing the infrastructure, with which tools and with what intent.
report.closing_body: The value of a honeypot lies in early detection: observing attacker behaviour in a controlled environment makes it possible to anticipate threats before they reach production systems. Most of the traffic any internet-exposed asset receives is mass automated scanning; the goal is not to eliminate it, but to keep it monitored. We recommend reviewing this report periodically. For exploit detection, per-IP behavioral scoring, threat intelligence and interactive protocol traps, see Heimdall Pro. Report generated automatically by Heimdall Community · AllSafe Security Solutions.

help.decoys.d: The fake page shown to whoever reaches the honeypot. Choosing the decoy well is half the work: the more believable and the closer it looks to something this organisation would actually run, the longer the attacker stays and the more they leave on record.
help.decoys.k1: The active decoy is the one served on ports 80 and 443, and it switches live with no restart
help.decoys.k2: The Community edition ships the fixed decoys; creating your own with the wizard is a Pro feature
help.decoys.k3: Switching decoy is recorded in Audit, because it changes what the attacker sees
help.decoys.k4: No decoy ever authenticates: it always rejects, and stores the username and password that were tried
help.report.d: The summary of the period, meant to be shown rather than analysed. It carries a plain-language verdict, the numbers that matter and the source tables, and exports to a branded PDF to attach to a report or leave on a table.
help.report.k1: The verdict comes from what was captured: calm, attention or alert, depending on exploitation attempts and campaigns
help.report.k2: Pick the range before exporting, because the PDF carries what you are looking at
help.report.k3: It is written for someone who does not work with the system every day
help.audit.d: A record of who did what inside Heimdall, with user and date. These are not the captured attacks, which live in Events: this is the actions of the people who administer the system.
help.audit.k1: Sensitive changes are recorded: decoy, decoy ports, threat intel keys, users, 2FA and event deletion
help.audit.k2: It is the record an audit asks for to show that changes are controlled
help.audit.k3: It cannot be edited or deleted from the interface, on purpose
help.map.d: Where what reaches the decoy comes from. Bubble size is the number of attempts and colour the predominant event type. It is the view that best communicates the problem to a non-technical audience.
help.map.k1: Origin is IP geolocation: it points at a country, it does not identify a person
help.map.k2: An IP can sit behind a VPN or proxy, so the country is not always the attacker's
help.map.k3: The time range changes the map: 24 hours shows what is happening, 30 days shows the pattern
help.users.d: Who can enter the panel and what they can do. The honeypot only captures, but the panel shows captured credentials and IPs, so access is limited like in any system holding sensitive data.
help.users.k1: Admin configures everything; analyst operates; auditor and viewer only look
help.users.k2: Blocking a user invalidates their open sessions immediately, not when the token expires
help.users.k3: 2FA can be reset for a user who lost their phone, and it is recorded in Audit
help.eventtypes.d: How Heimdall catalogues each attempt, from the most serious to the harmless: EXPLOIT, BRUTE, PORTSCAN, SCAN, BOT, HUMAN, RECON, RESEARCH and CRAWLER. The category sets the event score, so telling them apart properly is what makes the panel mean anything.
help.eventtypes.k1: CRAWLER is Googlebot or your monitoring: it scores 5 and does not add to the IP score, because it is not a threat
help.eventtypes.k2: RESEARCH is Shodan or Censys cataloguing what is exposed: exposure, not a targeted attack
help.eventtypes.k3: HUMAN requires headers a browser sends on its own; the user-agent is not enough, since it is faked in one line
help.eventtypes.k4: The requested path outranks the user-agent: whoever asks for /.env is scanning even if it claims to be Googlebot
help.eventtypes.k5: Each term is detailed in the Guide, with what to do in each case
help.threatintel.d: What external sources know about the IPs that visited you. An IP already reported for abuse or known as a Tor exit node weighs differently from one appearing for the first time.
help.threatintel.k1: The derived reputation condenses several sources into one reading: clean, suspicious, malicious or Tor
help.threatintel.k2: Community enriches one IP at a time, on demand. Batch and automatic enrichment are Pro
help.threatintel.k3: Community uses the keyless sources: ASN, Tor exit nodes, FeodoTracker and C2-Tracker
